sources.description:
I am an LLM researcher working on optimization and efficient training of neural networks. My current research includes low-rank pretraining, spectral regularization, parameter-efficient fine-tuning, and reducing the memory cost of language-model training.

I study how optimization and regularization affect the singular-value spectra and effective rank of weight matrices. I am interested in spectral weight decay, nuclear-norm regularization, proximal methods, and Newton-Schulz approximations. A central question is whether training can make a model easier to compress with low-rank factorization while preserving its quality. Related questions concern generalization and memorization under label noise.

Another research direction is optimization for LoRA and other low-rank parameterizations. Relevant topics include Muon-style matrix updates, optimization of factorized weights, rebalancing, spectral constraints, and convergence analysis. I want to understand both the geometry of these updates and their practical behavior when fine-tuning language models.

I also work on memory-efficient LLM pretraining. Relevant methods include low-rank gradient and optimizer-state representations, GaLore, Frugal-style methods, and low-precision optimizer states such as FP8. I am interested in their tradeoffs between model quality, training memory, throughput, and communication cost, including how those tradeoffs change with model scale.

As a secondary current interest, I am building an AI research digest agent with a handwritten harness. Relevant work includes explicit context management, structured LLM decisions, application-controlled tools, and paper retrieval and relevance ranking using lexical or embedding-based methods.

I have not specified hard topic exclusions for this digest.

passages.text: Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) often underperforms full fine-tuning, especially in heterogeneous and continual-learning settings in which substantial forgetting occurs. In general, it suffers from an undesirable learning–forgetting trade-off across diverse fine-tuning settings. We identify a potential contributor: LoRA adapters, especially high-rank ones, frequently fail to realize the available capacity afforded by the configured rank. Specifically, we find that standard LoRA updates have effective rank far below their configured rank, limiting how broadly the update energy is distributed. Therefore, we propose training mechanisms that optimize the original objective while maximizing adapter effective rank. Our main method adds a simple, stable, differentiable, and SVD-free Rényi-2 effective-rank regularizer to the language-modeling loss. We also connect capacity maximization to norm-bounded updates. In mixed-domain rank sweeps on three models evaluated with multiple random seeds, a penalty weight of λ = 0.01 \lambda=0.01 lowers mean Wiki perplexity at every tested rank of at least 16 16 relative to unpenalized LoRA. Mean training perplexity improves or increases by at most 0.02 0.02 in all but one model–rank comparison. Single-task and scheduling experiments further show that the balance between learning and retention depends on the configuration. We also observe that several LoRA variants in the literature also suffer from the identified capacity issue, and our approach provides a complementary axis of improvement to LoRA-based parameter-efficient fine-tuning. matches.abstract_excerpt: Language-model post-training modifies weights through cumulative updates and successive displacements, yet existing studies report seemingly conflicting spectral properties: nearly full-rank updates and low stable-rank changes. inspect:2611.11752.question: For OLMo-2-7B post-training weight updates, what do full SVD measurements show about stable rank versus rank needed to retain 80% energy, which layers and checkpoints were measured, and what limitations or controls bear on low-rank compression?

passages.text: Language-model post-training changes a model’s behavior by changing its weights. Supervised fine-tuning ( sft ) learns from demonstration responses, while reinforcement learning from verifiable rewards ( rlvr ) learns from sampled responses scored by an automatic checker. Weight-space measurements describe how these procedures alter a pretrained model and inform methods that operate on weight differences, including task arithmetic and low-rank adaptation ( Ilharco et al., 2023 ; Hu et al., 2022 ) . Interpreting those measurements requires separating the mathematical object being measured from the functional applied to it. That distinction matters when comparing recent accounts of post-training geometry. Mukherjee et al. (2025) report sparse, nearly full-algebraic-rank rlvr updates. Zhu et al. (2025) analyze update localization, numerical precision, and alignment with principal weight subspaces. Shen et al. (2026) compare cumulative updates in on-policy distillation, rlvr , and sft , reporting low stable rank for distillation and the rlvr endpoint. These studies characterize different aspects of adaptation. Yet their rank descriptions can appear incompatible if algebraic rank, stable rank, and energy coverage are treated as interchangeable. A comparison on the same update matrix is needed to determine what each description actually implies. We address this question with an explicit spectral construction and full-spectrum measurements of selected updates.

Even a complete endpoint spectrum leaves a second question unanswered. It does not determine whether consecutive training displacements reinforce or oppose one another. Analyses of full weight matrices ( He & Cao, 2025 ) and trajectory-level linear trends ( Wang et al., 2026 ) provide complementary information, but neither an endpoint change nor a fitted trend determines the inner products between consecutive finite displacements. We therefore measure direction at specified checkpoint widths and separations. These measurements describe local alignment on the saved checkpoint grid. Differences in trajectory alignment raise a third question. How does the advantage estimator affect the direction of weight updates under a shared training schedule? We investigate this question through a controlled comparison of group-relative advantages and a learned critic with generalized advantage estimation. Holding the actor schedule and sampled prompt stream fixed connects the observed geometry to a specific change in the training procedure. These investigations provide complementary views of post-training geometry. Spectral analysis characterizes how the cumulative weight change is distributed across singular directions, while trajectory analysis examines how successive weight changes interact during training. The controlled comparison then investigates whether changing the advantage system alters these directional relationships. Together, these measurements distinguish the structure of the final update from the geometry of the path taken to reach it.

The spectral and trajectory results describe complementary aspects of adaptation. Stable rank measures concentration around the leading singular value, while energy-threshold rank measures the breadth of the spectrum needed to retain a specified energy fraction. Consecutive-displacement cosine adds information about how successive changes interact. The public trajectories show anti-alignment across several RLVR recipes, and the controlled study demonstrates that the advantage system affects alignment magnitude under a shared actor schedule. The rank reconciliation explains how the reported spectral descriptions coexist. The power-law construction establishes this compatibility analytically, and the full decompositions demonstrate it on selected updates. Its practical implication is that a small stable rank can accompany substantial energy outside a low-rank approximation. Assessing the task-level value of that energy requires evaluating models after spectral truncation. The public survey measures aggregated changes on each release’s native checkpoint grid. Differences in schedules, exposure budgets, storage precision, and related stages limit causal comparisons across releases. The supervised study spans four model families under one data mixture and schedule, with the FP32 follow-up covering two Llama seeds. Its negative Mistral and FP32 Llama pairs show why trajectory sign should be interpreted together with the model and numerical training configuration. The controlled RL study covers one 1B initialization, one task source, one shared trainer, and three paired seeds. Its seed-level intervals characterize variation within that setting.

The controlled intervention combines critic fitting, GAE, and advantage normalization, so its effect applies to that package. Generated-token exposure remains policy-dependent, and the small held-out diagnostic shows no consistent performance improvement. Both local arms have higher mean alignment than the public RLVR trajectories. Identifying the source of this difference requires interventions within the production implementation, with matched exposure and adequate task evaluation. Full-SVD validation covers fourteen matrices selected by shape and layer position. The resulting accuracy measurements apply to this sample. All geometric quantities describe stored checkpoint weights, whose numerical precision affects apparent support sparsity and small displacements.

passages.text: Second-order optimizers ( e.g., Shampoo, SOAP) have emerged as compelling alternatives to Adam/AdamW and promise faster per-step convergence than AdamW in transformer training. However, they still remain costly in practice, and even SOAP still pays substantial optimizer-state memory and eigendecomposition overhead. We ask whether the benefits of SOAP can be retained at nearly the efficiency of AdamW. In this paper, we answer yes with a lightweight SOAP variant, Factored One-sided Adam-Moment (FOAM). The path to practical impact is twofold: first, FOAM employs input-only preconditioning, dropping the output-side Kronecker factor to reduce memory and remove one eigendecomposition. The Kronecker structure of the Hessian shows that this is exact for a diagonal output-side curvature and nearly lossless for a near-diagonal one, as we observe empirically. Second, FOAM replaces SOAP’s dense rotated second moment with a factored Adam-moment estimator based on row-by-column statistics. Under the K-FAC Fisher assumption with a diagonal output curvature, this estimator exactly recovers SOAP’s dense second moment, and we measure only a 15–20% K-FAC violation, with negligible effect on the update. Our empirical results support the claim that FOAM matches strong SOAP and Muon baselines in validation loss across scales of large language model (LLM) pre-training, uses half of SOAP’s optimizer state, runs at Muon-class wall-clock time, and retains robustness across a three-fold learning-rate range. The results hold from 124M to 760M parameters, demonstrating that SOAP’s gains need not require SOAP’s cost. Temporary changes during early training are known to have lasting effects on the learned solution ( Achille et al., 2017 ; Frankle et al., 2020 ) , and prior work has shown that regularization can matter disproportionately during early learning ( Golatkar et al., 2019 ) . We study a different aspect of this phenomenon: the effect of a temporary intervention can continue to evolve after the intervention has ended, to the point that its sign or ranking changes at later checkpoints. This creates a basic problem for evaluating temporary optimization schedules. Such schedules are usually specified by an update rule and the interval over which it is applied. But when the intervention ends, the treated and reference runs generally enter the subsequent phase with different parameters and optimizer states. Their loss difference can therefore continue to evolve even though their explicit update rules are again identical. Evaluating an intervention when it is removed can consequently select a schedule that is inferior at the intended final training budget—or reject one that will eventually be beneficial.

We study this phenomenon using temporary weight decay in Muon-trained decoder-only Transformers. Weight decay provides a particularly controlled setting: turning it off cleanly separates its direct shrinkage from the training state it leaves behind. Muon also provides a useful connection between weight norms and subsequent optimization. Its matrix updates have approximately controlled magnitude, so for a given projected update norm, reducing the weight norm increases the update size relative to the current weights ( Jordan et al., 2024 ; Kosson et al., 2023 ; Wen et al., 2026 ; Liu et al., 2026 ) . Temporary decay can therefore alter subsequent optimization even after its coefficient has returned to zero. We ask two related questions: Central question. How should a temporary optimization intervention be evaluated, and what aspects of the training state carry its effect after the intervention is removed? We address the first question by varying when decay starts, how long it lasts, and when its effect is evaluated. Across models from 162M to 1.4B parameters, moving a fixed-duration decay window from early to late training reverses its final effect: early windows improve final loss, whereas a window beginning at 60 % 60\% of training hurts. At 405M, even among beneficial early schedules, the ranking changes depending on whether they are compared at a common final training budget or after the same amount of post-removal training. At 162M, changing window duration also changes final loss substantially even when total multiplicative shrinkage is approximately matched. These results separate three notions that are often conflated: when an intervention acts, how long the model trains after it is removed, and the final budget at which it is evaluated.

We address the second question by examining what remains different after decay is removed. Early decay leaves a persistent weight-norm deficit, which keeps relative steps larger than in the no-decay run long after both models resume the same update rule. An approximate recurrence accounts for the slow convergence of these relative-step trajectories. An opposite perturbation—boosting the learning rate early—raises weight norms and leaves relative steps smaller after the boost ends, as predicted by the same account. More directly, fixed-norm replays using the measured relative-step trajectories reproduce the performance ordering and a similar loss difference; swapping trajectories at the end of the decay window shows that most of the replay advantage arises from the altered steps after decay has ended. These experiments explain how an early intervention can continue to modify optimization after removal, although they do not establish that norms are the only persistent state or explain why a particular relative-step trajectory is beneficial. Together, these experiments characterize both the evaluation consequences of delayed optimization effects and one mechanism by which an early intervention can remain active through the state it leaves behind.

passages.text: Transmitting LoRA adapters to rollout workers can bottleneck distributed on-policy post-training over bandwidth-constrained networks. Lowering the training rank may limit the capacity a workload needs, while adaptive optimizer updates are difficult to compress. Rollout workers can instead reconstruct updates from gradients by maintaining replicated optimizer states. We introduce HiLo , a compressor-agnostic framework that replaces parameter transmission with compressed gradient dissemination and local optimizer replay. By applying the same decoded gradients, the learner and workers maintain consistent policy states at the same version under reproducible execution. We further develop Spar , a budget-aware gradient compressor that combines spectral truncation, adaptive rank allocation and error feedback to decouple training rank from communication cost. passages.text: Parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) aims to preserve adaptation quality while reducing training costs. We propose SCALAR , which achieves performance comparable to LoRA with substantially fewer trainable parameters, lower peak training memory, and higher throughput. SCALAR constructs a fixed input basis from task activations and assigns a random output dictionary to each input direction. Fine-tuning learns only layer-specific scalar coefficients, reducing gradient and optimizer-state storage. Grouped computation aggregates output atoms before applying the adapter to token activations, while dictionary sharing across compatible layers reduces fixed-basis storage. Experiments on commonsense reasoning, mathematical reasoning, code generation, and knowledge evaluation after instruction tuning demonstrate effective adaptation at small trainable budgets. On commonsense reasoning, SCALAR achieves accuracy comparable to LoRA with about 4% of its trainable parameters. System measurements on Qwen2.5-7B show 20% lower peak training memory and 6% higher throughput than LoRA. The combination of adaptation quality, a compact trainable state, and training efficiency makes SCALAR a promising approach to resource-constrained fine-tuning. 1 1 footnotetext: Work done during an internship at OPPO AI-Center. 1 1 footnotetext: National University of Defense Technology. Contact: suntao.saltfish@outlook.com 2 2 footnotetext: OPPO AI center

Existing methods primarily optimize storage, retrieval, or compression, but the memories most semantically relevant to the current state are not necessarily those that most improve the agent’s action. We introduce MemCredit , a decision-centric memory framework that shifts memory selection from semantic relevance to decision utility . MemCredit estimates the state-, reference-context-, and policy-conditional marginal contribution of individual memories through controlled counterfactual interventions, and distills these intervention-derived credits into a lightweight utility estimator. At inference time, semantic relevance is used only for high-recall candidate generation, while predicted utility arbitrates which memories are retained under a fixed token budget, without modifying the underlying agent policy or requiring additional environment interaction. We evaluate MemCredit on ALFWorld and WebShop against representative memory baselines. On ALFWorld, MemCredit achieves 86.57 % 86.57\% SR@50 under a 500-token historical-memory budget, compared with 65.67 % 65.67\% for BM25 retrieval. Counterfactual analysis further shows that memory utility is sparse, strongly state dependent, and poorly captured by semantic relevance. These results suggest that decision utility provides a more effective principle than relevance alone for long-horizon agent memory management.

It is related to recent experience- and skill-based agents that evaluate reusable knowledge through downstream outcomes ( Xia et al., 2026 ; Tu et al., 2026 ) , but operates at the granularity of individual memories. Controlled intervention experiments support this distinction (Sec. 4.3 ; Table 3 and Figure 5 ). Motivated by these findings, we introduce MemCredit , a framework for decision-time memory arbitration in long-horizon agents. MemCredit decomposes interaction histories into atomic memories and uses controlled counterfactual interventions to estimate their marginal decision contributions. The resulting credits supervise a lightweight utility estimator, amortizing the cost of counterfactual evaluation. At inference time, MemCredit separates candidate recall from memory arbitration : semantic relevance retrieves a broad candidate pool, while predicted utility determines which memories are retained under a fixed token budget. The underlying agent policy remains unchanged and requires no additional environment interaction at deployment. We evaluate MemCredit on ALFWorld ( Shridhar et al., 2021 ) and WebShop ( Yao et al., 2022 ) . On ALFWorld, MemCredit achieves 86.57 % 86.57\% SR@50 under a 500-token historical-memory budget, outperforming BM25 retrieval by 20.90 20.90 percentage points. With a 750-token budget, it reaches 90.30 % 90.30\% SR@50, compared with 81.34 % 81.34\% for BM25, showing larger gains under tighter context constraints. On WebShop, MemCredit achieves the highest task score of 0.612 0.612 while using only 152.1 152.1 memory tokens per decision. Compared with MemArbiter, the strongest non-MemCredit baseline, it improves the score from 0.586 0.586 to 0.612 0.612 while using about 2.8 × 2.8\times fewer memory tokens; relative to BM25, memory usage is reduced by approximately 3.9 × 3.9\times . • We formulate decision-time memory credit assignment , distinguishing semantic relevance from the state- and policy-conditional marginal contribution of an individual memory, and show that such utility is sparse, state dependent, and poorly captured by relevance. • We propose MemCredit , which estimates fine-grained memory credit through controlled counterfactual intervention and distills it into an amortized utility estimator for budget-aware memory arbitration. • We demonstrate on ALFWorld and WebShop that separating relevance-based candidate recall from utility-based arbitration improves both task performance and context efficiency, especially under tight historical-memory budgets. Agent memory supports long-horizon interaction through experience retrieval ( Park et al., 2023 ) , long-term storage ( Zhong et al., 2024 ) , tiered context management ( Packer et al., 2023 ) , and evolving memory structures ( Xu et al., 2025 ) . Recent methods further compress trajectories into structured states ( Zhu et al., 2026 ) , learn bounded memory updates ( Luo et al., 2026 ) , or select compressed blocks using the query and working memory ( Chen et al., 2026 ) . MemArbiter ( Dong et al., 2026 ) addresses the Memory–Action Gap : retrievable information may still fail to guide actions. It organizes history into functional banks and controls memory presentation through demand, relevance, and temporal signals. Its arbitration uses predefined signals rather than intervention-derived memory credits. Closer approaches explicitly evaluate memory utility. CMI ( Srivastava, 2026 ) scores memories through controlled interventions in conversational tasks. CICL ( Guan et al., 2026 ) estimates decision-oriented utility and assembles selected evidence into budgeted memory cards. MeClear ( Yang et al., 2026 ) combines leave-one-out screening with sampled Shapley attribution to capture interactions and suppress harmful memories. MemCredit focuses on state-conditioned, item-level credit assignment for sequential decisions. It collects credits through paired replay from matched environment states under a fixed action policy, then trains a lightweight estimator for token-budgeted selection without additional runtime environment interaction. Single-removal attribution can mask redundancy among interacting memories; Sec. 3.4 discusses how conditional reference contexts mitigate this.

We introduced MemCredit, a decision-utility-based memory framework for long-horizon agents. Rather than treating semantic relevance as the primary criterion for memory selection, MemCredit estimates the context-conditional marginal contribution of individual memories through counterfactual credit assignment, while keeping the action policy frozen and avoiding additional environment interaction at deployment. Experiments on ALFWorld and WebShop show that this principle improves memory arbitration under limited context budgets. Our analysis further reveals that decision utility is sparse, strongly state dependent, and only weakly captured by semantic relevance. These findings suggest that future agent memory systems should optimize not only what information is retrieved, but which memories are most consequential for the decisions that follow.

SCALAR's memory and throughput measurements are for Qwen2.5-7B fine-tuning on two NVIDIA H20 GPUs; results need not generalize to other systems.

2611.11752:b899646e763348f79069dbc35119d.question: For OLMo-2-7B post-training weight updates, what do full SVD measurements show about stable rank versus rank needed to retain 80% energy, which layers and checkpoints were measured, and what limitations or controls bear on low-rank compression?

passages.text: Language-model post-training changes a model’s behavior by changing its weights. Supervised fine-tuning ( sft ) learns from demonstration responses, while reinforcement learning from verifiable rewards ( rlvr ) learns from sampled responses scored by an automatic checker. Weight-space measurements describe how these procedures alter a pretrained model and inform methods that operate on weight differences, including task arithmetic and low-rank adaptation ( Ilharco et al., 2023 ; Hu et al., 2022 ) . Interpreting those measurements requires separating the mathematical object being measured from the functional applied to it. That distinction matters when comparing recent accounts of post-training geometry. Mukherjee et al. (2025) report sparse, nearly full-algebraic-rank rlvr updates. Zhu et al. (2025) analyze update localization, numerical precision, and alignment with principal weight subspaces. Shen et al. (2026) compare cumulative updates in on-policy distillation, rlvr , and sft , reporting low stable rank for distillation and the rlvr endpoint. These studies characterize different aspects of adaptation. Yet their rank descriptions can appear incompatible if algebraic rank, stable rank, and energy coverage are treated as interchangeable. A comparison on the same update matrix is needed to determine what each description actually implies. We address this question with an explicit spectral construction and full-spectrum measurements of selected updates.

Even a complete endpoint spectrum leaves a second question unanswered. It does not determine whether consecutive training displacements reinforce or oppose one another. Analyses of full weight matrices ( He & Cao, 2025 ) and trajectory-level linear trends ( Wang et al., 2026 ) provide complementary information, but neither an endpoint change nor a fitted trend determines the inner products between consecutive finite displacements. We therefore measure direction at specified checkpoint widths and separations. These measurements describe local alignment on the saved checkpoint grid. Differences in trajectory alignment raise a third question. How does the advantage estimator affect the direction of weight updates under a shared training schedule? We investigate this question through a controlled comparison of group-relative advantages and a learned critic with generalized advantage estimation. Holding the actor schedule and sampled prompt stream fixed connects the observed geometry to a specific change in the training procedure. These investigations provide complementary views of post-training geometry. Spectral analysis characterizes how the cumulative weight change is distributed across singular directions, while trajectory analysis examines how successive weight changes interact during training. The controlled comparison then investigates whether changing the advantage system alters these directional relationships. Together, these measurements distinguish the structure of the final update from the geometry of the path taken to reach it.

The spectral and trajectory results describe complementary aspects of adaptation. Stable rank measures concentration around the leading singular value, while energy-threshold rank measures the breadth of the spectrum needed to retain a specified energy fraction. Consecutive-displacement cosine adds information about how successive changes interact. The public trajectories show anti-alignment across several RLVR recipes, and the controlled study demonstrates that the advantage system affects alignment magnitude under a shared actor schedule. The rank reconciliation explains how the reported spectral descriptions coexist. The power-law construction establishes this compatibility analytically, and the full decompositions demonstrate it on selected updates. Its practical implication is that a small stable rank can accompany substantial energy outside a low-rank approximation. Assessing the task-level value of that energy requires evaluating models after spectral truncation. The public survey measures aggregated changes on each release’s native checkpoint grid. Differences in schedules, exposure budgets, storage precision, and related stages limit causal comparisons across releases. The supervised study spans four model families under one data mixture and schedule, with the FP32 follow-up covering two Llama seeds. Its negative Mistral and FP32 Llama pairs show why trajectory sign should be interpreted together with the model and numerical training configuration. The controlled RL study covers one 1B initialization, one task source, one shared trainer, and three paired seeds. Its seed-level intervals characterize variation within that setting.

The controlled intervention combines critic fitting, GAE, and advantage normalization, so its effect applies to that package. Generated-token exposure remains policy-dependent, and the small held-out diagnostic shows no consistent performance improvement. Both local arms have higher mean alignment than the public RLVR trajectories. Identifying the source of this difference requires interventions within the production implementation, with matched exposure and adequate task evaluation. Full-SVD validation covers fourteen matrices selected by shape and layer position. The resulting accuracy measurements apply to this sample. All geometric quantities describe stored checkpoint weights, whose numerical precision affects apparent support sparsity and small displacements.

In this work, we studied language-model post-training by separating the structure of cumulative weight updates from the directions of successive training displacements. Our power-law construction showed that low stable rank and large fixed-energy rank are mathematically compatible, and full decompositions verified this separation in selected OLMo-2-7B updates. A dominant singular value can therefore coexist with hundreds of components needed to retain most of an update’s energy. This distinction clarifies why different rank measures can give contrasting descriptions of the same matrix. Trajectory measurements add information about how successive weight changes interact. All 131 measured adjacent pairs across nine public RLVR stages from the OLMo-2, OLMoE, and Olmo-3 releases had negative cosine on their native checkpoint grids, including PPO and GRPO releases. Together, these findings support a more precise account of post-training geometry. 2611.16905:1ae86ffed6db6a028abaac9bb0ac8.question: In LLM pretraining experiments, which model scales and baselines (AdamW, SOAP, Muon) are compared with FOAM, and what are the measured optimizer-state memory, wall-clock time, and validation-loss trade-offs under matched training budgets?

passages.text: Second-order optimizers ( e.g., Shampoo, SOAP) have emerged as compelling alternatives to Adam/AdamW and promise faster per-step convergence than AdamW in transformer training. However, they still remain costly in practice, and even SOAP still pays substantial optimizer-state memory and eigendecomposition overhead. We ask whether the benefits of SOAP can be retained at nearly the efficiency of AdamW. In this paper, we answer yes with a lightweight SOAP variant, Factored One-sided Adam-Moment (FOAM). The path to practical impact is twofold: first, FOAM employs input-only preconditioning, dropping the output-side Kronecker factor to reduce memory and remove one eigendecomposition. The Kronecker structure of the Hessian shows that this is exact for a diagonal output-side curvature and nearly lossless for a near-diagonal one, as we observe empirically. Second, FOAM replaces SOAP’s dense rotated second moment with a factored Adam-moment estimator based on row-by-column statistics. Under the K-FAC Fisher assumption with a diagonal output curvature, this estimator exactly recovers SOAP’s dense second moment, and we measure only a 15–20% K-FAC violation, with negligible effect on the update. Our empirical results support the claim that FOAM matches strong SOAP and Muon baselines in validation loss across scales of large language model (LLM) pre-training, uses half of SOAP’s optimizer state, runs at Muon-class wall-clock time, and retains robustness across a three-fold learning-rate range. The results hold from 124M to 760M parameters, demonstrating that SOAP’s gains need not require SOAP’s cost. Concretely, our approach is built on two structural simplifications: input-only preconditioning and a factored Adam-Moment update. The first simplification drops the output-side factor L L and retains only the input-side factor R R , eliminating its m 2 m^{2} memory and one of the two eigendecompositions. Its justification follows from the Kronecker structure of the Hessian, in which all output rows of an affine layer share the same input-side outer product x ​ x ⊤ xx^{\top} [ 25 ] , while the Hessian of transformer layers is empirically near-block-diagonal along output neurons or heads [ 50 ] , making the input-only form the natural one-sided approximation. The second simplification replaces the dense rotated second moment with a row-and-column factored estimator, r ∈ ℝ m r\in\mathbb{R}^{m} and c ∈ ℝ n c\in\mathbb{R}^{n} , with trace normalization, reducing the buffer size from m ​ n mn to m + n m+n . Under the K-FAC Fisher assumption [ 35 ] with a diagonal output curvature, this estimator exactly recovers SOAP’s dense second moment, and the K-FAC part holds to a 15 15 – 20 % 20\% relative error in practice. Together, these simplifications reduce SOAP’s optimizer state from 2 ​ m ​ n + 2 ​ m 2 + 2 ​ n 2 2mn+2m^{2}+2n^{2} to m ​ n + 2 ​ n 2 + m + n mn+2n^{2}+m+n and the amortized eigendecomposition count from two to one. We call the resulting method FOAM ( F actored O ne-sided A dam- M oment).

Figure 1 highlights FOAM’s main advantages. Temporary changes during early training are known to have lasting effects on the learned solution ( Achille et al., 2017 ; Frankle et al., 2020 ) , and prior work has shown that regularization can matter disproportionately during early learning ( Golatkar et al., 2019 ) . We study a different aspect of this phenomenon: the effect of a temporary intervention can continue to evolve after the intervention has ended, to the point that its sign or ranking changes at later checkpoints. This creates a basic problem for evaluating temporary optimization schedules. Such schedules are usually specified by an update rule and the interval over which it is applied. But when the intervention ends, the treated and reference runs generally enter the subsequent phase with different parameters and optimizer states. Their loss difference can therefore continue to evolve even though their explicit update rules are again identical. Evaluating an intervention when it is removed can consequently select a schedule that is inferior at the intended final training budget—or reject one that will eventually be beneficial.

We study this phenomenon using temporary weight decay in Muon-trained decoder-only Transformers. Weight decay provides a particularly controlled setting: turning it off cleanly separates its direct shrinkage from the training state it leaves behind. Muon also provides a useful connection between weight norms and subsequent optimization. Its matrix updates have approximately controlled magnitude, so for a given projected update norm, reducing the weight norm increases the update size relative to the current weights ( Jordan et al., 2024 ; Kosson et al., 2023 ; Wen et al., 2026 ; Liu et al., 2026 ) . Temporary decay can therefore alter subsequent optimization even after its coefficient has returned to zero. We ask two related questions: Central question. How should a temporary optimization intervention be evaluated, and what aspects of the training state carry its effect after the intervention is removed? We address the first question by varying when decay starts, how long it lasts, and when its effect is evaluated. Across models from 162M to 1.4B parameters, moving a fixed-duration decay window from early to late training reverses its final effect: early windows improve final loss, whereas a window beginning at 60 % 60\% of training hurts. At 405M, even among beneficial early schedules, the ranking changes depending on whether they are compared at a common final training budget or after the same amount of post-removal training. At 162M, changing window duration also changes final loss substantially even when total multiplicative shrinkage is approximately matched. These results separate three notions that are often conflated: when an intervention acts, how long the model trains after it is removed, and the final budget at which it is evaluated.

We address the second question by examining what remains different after decay is removed. Early decay leaves a persistent weight-norm deficit, which keeps relative steps larger than in the no-decay run long after both models resume the same update rule. An approximate recurrence accounts for the slow convergence of these relative-step trajectories. An opposite perturbation—boosting the learning rate early—raises weight norms and leaves relative steps smaller after the boost ends, as predicted by the same account. More directly, fixed-norm replays using the measured relative-step trajectories reproduce the performance ordering and a similar loss difference; swapping trajectories at the end of the decay window shows that most of the replay advantage arises from the altered steps after decay has ended. These experiments explain how an early intervention can continue to modify optimization after removal, although they do not establish that norms are the only persistent state or explain why a particular relative-step trajectory is beneficial. Together, these experiments characterize both the evaluation consequences of delayed optimization effects and one mechanism by which an early intervention can remain active through the state it leaves behind.

passages.text: Transmitting LoRA adapters to rollout workers can bottleneck distributed on-policy post-training over bandwidth-constrained networks. Lowering the training rank may limit the capacity a workload needs, while adaptive optimizer updates are difficult to compress. Rollout workers can instead reconstruct updates from gradients by maintaining replicated optimizer states. We introduce HiLo , a compressor-agnostic framework that replaces parameter transmission with compressed gradient dissemination and local optimizer replay. By applying the same decoded gradients, the learner and workers maintain consistent policy states at the same version under reproducible execution. We further develop Spar , a budget-aware gradient compressor that combines spectral truncation, adaptive rank allocation and error feedback to decouple training rank from communication cost. We propose SCALAR , which achieves performance comparable to LoRA with substantially fewer trainable parameters, lower peak training memory, and higher throughput. SCALAR constructs a fixed input basis from task activations and assigns a random output dictionary to each input direction. Fine-tuning learns only layer-specific scalar coefficients, reducing gradient and optimizer-state storage. Grouped computation aggregates output atoms before applying the adapter to token activations, while dictionary sharing across compatible layers reduces fixed-basis storage. Experiments on commonsense reasoning, mathematical reasoning, code generation, and knowledge evaluation after instruction tuning demonstrate effective adaptation at small trainable budgets. On commonsense reasoning, SCALAR achieves accuracy comparable to LoRA with about 4% of its trainable parameters. System measurements on Qwen2.5-7B show 20% lower peak training memory and 6% higher throughput than LoRA. These results suggest that decision utility provides a more effective principle than relevance alone for long-horizon agent memory management.

CICL ( Guan et al., 2026 ) estimates decision-oriented utility and assembles selected evidence into budgeted memory cards. MeClear ( Yang et al., 2026 ) combines leave-one-out screening with sampled Shapley attribution to capture interactions and suppress harmful memories. Large language model (LLM) agents increasingly operate over long Web interaction histories, making memory management critical for reliable and efficient decision making. Existing methods primarily optimize storage, retrieval, or compression, but the memories most semantically relevant to the current state are not necessarily those that most improve the agent’s action. We introduce MemCredit , a decision-centric memory framework that shifts memory selection from semantic relevance to decision utility . MemCredit estimates the state-, reference-context-, and policy-conditional marginal contribution of individual memories through controlled counterfactual interventions, and distills these intervention-derived credits into a lightweight utility estimator. At inference time, semantic relevance is used only for high-recall candidate generation, while predicted utility arbitrates which memories are retained under a fixed token budget, without modifying the underlying agent policy or requiring additional environment interaction. We evaluate MemCredit on ALFWorld and WebShop against representative memory baselines. On ALFWorld, MemCredit achieves 86.57 % 86.57\% SR@50 under a 500-token historical-memory budget, compared with 65.67 % 65.67\% for BM25 retrieval. Counterfactual analysis further shows that memory utility is sparse, strongly state dependent, and poorly captured by semantic relevance. These results suggest that decision utility provides a more effective principle than relevance alone for long-horizon agent memory management.

Agent memory supports long-horizon interaction through experience retrieval ( Park et al., 2023 ) , long-term storage ( Zhong et al., 2024 ) , tiered context management ( Packer et al., 2023 ) , and evolving memory structures ( Xu et al., 2025 ) . Recent methods further compress trajectories into structured states ( Zhu et al., 2026 ) , learn bounded memory updates ( Luo et al., 2026 ) , or select compressed blocks using the query and working memory ( Chen et al., 2026 ) . MemArbiter ( Dong et al., 2026 ) addresses the Memory–Action Gap : retrievable information may still fail to guide actions. It organizes history into functional banks and controls memory presentation through demand, relevance, and temporal signals. Its arbitration uses predefined signals rather than intervention-derived memory credits. Closer approaches explicitly evaluate memory utility. CMI ( Srivastava, 2026 ) scores memories through controlled interventions in conversational tasks. CICL ( Guan et al., 2026 ) estimates decision-oriented utility and assembles selected evidence into budgeted memory cards. MeClear ( Yang et al., 2026 ) combines leave-one-out screening with sampled Shapley attribution to capture interactions and suppress harmful memories. MemCredit focuses on state-conditioned, item-level credit assignment for sequential decisions. It collects credits through paired replay from matched environment states under a fixed action policy, then trains a lightweight estimator for token-budgeted selection without additional runtime environment interaction. Single-removal attribution can mask redundancy among interacting memories; Sec. 3.4 discusses how conditional reference contexts mitigate this.
